newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Little change seen in 97/98 world wheat crop - NAEGA.
newsitem.headline: Little change seen in 97/98 world wheat crop - NAEGA.

text.p: World wheat production in 1997/98 should be unchanged to slightly lower, with acreage declines in Canada, the U.S. and Argentina reacting to lower world wheat values, said the feedgrains marketing development manager of U.S. trade house Cargill.
Acreage in Australia is likely to be unchanged but much will depend on prices of wool and other alternative crops, Terry Garvert told an international wheat conference here.
Garvert was speaking as a member of the North American Export Grain Association (NAEGA) which represents 40 firms.

In the U.S., overall wheat acreage should drop between two to five percent with a two to four percent increase in hard red winter wheat, an eight to 10 percent decrease in soft red winter wheat and an eight to 11 percent increase in hard red spring wheat.
Area planted to soft white wheat should remain unchanged to slightly higher while durum acreage is expected to be down between five and 10 percent, Garvert said.
A new farm program with increased planting flexibility for the producer to switch from wheat to oilseeds may also have an effect, he added.

While it is very early to make a guesstimate, some private forecasts have projected a total U.S. crop somewhere around 68 million tonnes which would be around six million tonnes higher than in 1996/97 even with reduced planted acreage.
The primary reason would be more "normal" abandonments in winter wheat production assuming less winterkill after historic levels of 28 percent for HRW and 17 percent of SRW this year.
Soil moisture conditions are also optimal for the winter development of winter crops.
As far as exports from the current U.S crop are concerned, Garvert said he did not expect the U.S. Department of Agriculture to have an export enhancement program (EEP) through the winter months.

Open sales and commitments are already 18.6 million tonnes from the U.S. by the end of October, over 75 percent of projected exports of 24.9 million tonnes, leaving over half of the crop year to trade less than 25 percent of the remaining export projections.
On the import side, traditional big buyers are expected to reduce their purchases in the current year due to larger domestic crops.
The former Soviet Union is now seen brining in seven million tonnes of wheat, most of which however will come from former Soviet states. Third country imports may be as low as one million tonnes.
In China, a record crop of over 109 million tonnes means that purchases could decline to seven million tonnes or less.
"Obviously any change in these two would catch the market by surprise. It is not likely to happen," Garvert said.
Overall world wheat demand in 1996/7 is still expected to grow however by 21 million tonnes to a figure of around 571 million, up three to four percent over last year.
This will be due to heavy wheat feeding in the U.S. and other areas like Korea where wheat was fed in the June to September quarter due to very tight feedgrain situations.
This adds up to a projected increase in world wheat carryout stocks on a June 1, 1997 basis of over seven million tonnes, representing a stocks-to-use ratio of closer to 20 percent.

"This is a much more relaxed percentage and one the market will be more readily able to live with. It is not overburdensome but it does give the market more comfort with its stock situation," Garvert said.

The big question the market needs to have answered is who of the major five wheat producers (the U.S., Canada, Argentina, Australia and the E.U.) will provide the market function of "carrying" the increased carryout, he added.
-- Caroline Bulloch, Rio de Janeiro newsroom, 5521 5074151
